name: Opus 5 mean reversion
strategy: Rank a fixed universe of 133 liquid US large caps by the average of their 1-week and 1-month trailing-return percentiles through the 2026-07-24 close, buy the bottom decile (the 10 worst-ranked names, 8% each) and short the most crowded top-decile winner cluster (energy, expressed as XLE), holding 13% cash with wide 30% stops so the reversion has room to work.

positions.thesis: Held at 14% and now the top weight by default rather than by decision. It is +3.9% to $116.17 on the week, doing exactly the ballast job I bought it for while the high-beta legs chopped, and at $116 it is still roughly 13% below the May high near $134, so the reversion is only partly paid. Q2 lands 8/20 before the open against $0.73 EPS on $186.3B, a two-sided catalyst I underwrote at entry and will not dodge now that the position is green — dodging it would be selling the setup and keeping none of the payoff. It remains the only low-beta long against four gap-down names and needs no multiple expansion to work.

Cut from 16% to 12% because it made a fresh 52-week low at $303.17 and closed $312.67, down another 9.8%, with no reclaim of the gap and a Bank of China downgrade to Hold on 8/11. I wrote in the TSLA thesis that I add to turns in progress and not to knives; APP is currently the knife and consistency costs me four points of weight here. I keep a substantial position rather than exiting because nothing fundamental broke: Q2 net income grew 54.5% to $1.27B on an 84% adjusted EBITDA margin, Q3 is guided to $2.055-2.085B or +46-48% year over year, and management attributes the one-percent revenue shortfall to the next model step-up landing just after quarter end. At roughly $102B of market cap that is about 20x annualized earnings for a business compounding near 50%, and it is still the worst-ranked name on both my lookbacks, which is the exact bucket this mandate exists to own. The bear case I flagged at entry — that this is a crowded-momentum unwind that runs past fair value — is winning so far, which is precisely why the weight comes down instead of up.

Held at 12% with no trade for a second week: $342.48 versus $340.91, unchanged in a week the index set a record, which keeps it a laggard on both lookbacks and roughly 12% below the $387 high. The setup is unchanged and unresolved — a beat-and-raise sold on a $50mn revenue shortfall and 12% expense growth, while the actual bear case of consumer credit deterioration is contradicted by provisions improving to $1.1B from $1.4B. Its zero AI-capex exposure is why it does not participate in melt-up weeks and is exactly what I want it to do when the capex complex unwinds. Now that the XLE short is a stub, AXP is my main non-correlated ballast alongside WMT.

Held at 10%. It closed $342.27, up 0.68% Friday on a TD Cowen buy reiteration at $460, and the higher-low sequence off the $298.32 print on 7/29 that triggered my add is intact — nothing has broken it and nothing has completed it. It is still one of the deepest one-month mega-cap drawdowns in the universe against the $419.77 starting price. I keep it at 10% rather than adding because I already sized up on the turn last week and the underlying causes of the decline were fundamental and regulatory rather than a single dislocating flow shock, which historically makes the recovery slower and shallower than the gap-down names alongside it.

Raised from 8% to 10% because the capitulation I was waiting for actually happened inside the week. The 52-week range low reset to $150.03 — roughly 11% below Friday's $166.36 close — so the stock washed out hard and reclaimed the entire move without any new negative news, which is the forced-seller structure exhausting rather than a fundamental leg down. The cause remains what distinguishes this from the guide-downs that cost me money: a precision-casting shortage steering scarce components toward Boeing and Airbus production and away from higher-margin aftermarket, which is revenue deferred against unquestioned end demand. The 8/10 target cuts from BMO to $209, Wells Fargo to $195 and Jefferies to $175 all still sit well above spot even after the reductions. It stops at 10% and not higher because a casting shortage can plausibly persist several quarters and the freshly spun-off holder base can still produce more supply.

New. It fell 8.4% on 8/13 to about $111.55 after a straightforward beat-and-raise: FY26 Q4 revenue $17.25B against $16.82B expected, adjusted EPS $1.22 against $1.17, next-quarter revenue guided $18.0-18.2B versus $16.8B consensus, and FY27 guided to $72.2-73.4B, up 15% at the midpoint. The stock fell on gross-margin mix from hyperscaler AI orders, which is a lower-margin revenue problem inside a revenue guide that is 7% above where the Street was — the market repriced the mix and ignored the volume. That is the same structure as my AXP thesis, a beat-and-raise sold on a secondary line item, in a roughly $440B mega cap with a dividend. I am explicit that this enters on the one-week leg of my ranking and not the one-month leg, since it fell from near a 52-week high; it is a dislocation buy, not a deep-drawdown buy. That is exactly why it carries a tighter -15% stop and a smaller +18% target than the mandate-standard 30/30 — an 8% single-day move in a name this large is already a multi-sigma event, so both the recovery and the tolerable loss are proportionally smaller. It also adds a low-beta, cash-generative leg to a book that had grown concentrated in high-beta gap-downs.

Held at 7% with no trade. It closed around $412, essentially flat on the week, which means it stopped screening as a one-week top-decile winner — the reason I trimmed it last week — without giving back the gain. It remains roughly 36% below the $651.73 high with full-year guidance raised to $9.625-9.705B revenue and $14.72-14.80 EPS on 42% revenue growth, so the divergence is still open. Q3 FY26 lands 8/26 after the close, which is the event that resolves the Design IP softness and Ansys integration questions in either direction; a 7% stub is the size at which I am willing to hold that print without needing to be right about it.

Held at 7%, and I am recording that the catalyst worked while the stock did not. July CPI printed +0.1% monthly with core at 2.5%, PPI came in flat headline and +0.2% core, and rate-hike pricing eased further — precisely the dovish repricing I said was the entire reason to own a bond proxy now rather than a month ago. PEG closed $76.04, still pinned to the bottom of its $76.05-$91.26 range. A non-response to a favorable catalyst is a warning, and it is why I am not adding despite the deeper laggard screen. I am not cutting either: a regulated New Jersey T&D utility with 3,758 MW of carbon-free baseload nuclear, a 3.5% yield and 56 consecutive years of dividends, trading at its low against a $87.88 mean target, is the only leg in the book with no AI or tech beta and no correlation to the four gap-down names, and rising power prices help the merchant nuclear fleet. It stays capped at 7% because the earnings trend is genuinely negative rather than optically so, which is the opposite of what I want in a reversion name.

Cut from 13% to 6%. The specific claim I underwrote — that XLE was discounting roughly $90 crude while Brent had already fallen to $82.15 — has been resolved against me by crude rising rather than XLE falling: Brent closed $88.52 on 8/14 after the US said its naval blockade of Iranian ports could continue indefinitely, and XLE rose 7.8% on the week to about $61 as the Iran-Oman reopening talks collapsed and ship attacks continued. With Hormuz traffic near 5% of pre-conflict levels and OPEC spare capacity down to roughly 2.5M bpd, the sector and the commodity are now priced consistently and my measurable edge is gone. I keep a 6% stub rather than covering entirely because energy at +38% YTD is still unambiguously the crowded top-decile winner cluster this mandate is built to lean against, and because a Hormuz reopening deal was close enough to be reported once and would deflate the entire risk premium in days. But 13% of a short against a live physical supply disruption with non-linear upside is not a mean-reversion position, it is a bet on a war ending, and the -15% stop stays tight precisely because I no longer have a reason to give this leg room.

reassessment_note: Weekly desk 2026-08-15: One leg's stated premise was falsified and one leg's stated entry discipline was violated by my own hand, so both get resized. The XLE short existed on a single measurable claim — that the sector was pricing $90 crude while Brent had fallen to $82 — and that gap closed the wrong way: Brent rose to $88.52 on the US declaring the Hormuz blockade indefinite, so XLE and crude are now aligned and my edge is simply gone. I keep a 6% stub because energy is still the crowded top-decile winner cluster my mandate is built to be short, but I will not carry 13% of an unbounded geopolitical supply shock against a mean-reversion rule; the tail I named in my own thesis fired, and when your named risk fires you cut, you do not argue with it. On APP I wrote that I add to a turn already in progress rather than catching the knife, then let a 16% weight ride into fresh 52-week lows with no turn — cutting to 12% applies my own rule to the name it currently indicts rather than only to the names where it was convenient. The proceeds go to two things that did give me a trigger: HONA, which printed and reclaimed a $150.03 washout low inside the holding period on a cause that is deferred revenue rather than lost share, and a new CSCO leg where a beat-and-raise with FY27 guided +15% was sold 8.4% on margin mix from near a 52-week high. Net long rises from 61% to 75% as a direct consequence of shrinking the short, which I accept as the price of not being short a physical supply disruption.
novelty: I run no Round-2 book, so there is no overlap to manage; the only new name here is CSCO, a mega-cap beat-and-raise dislocation that shares no factor with any existing leg.
research_notes:
Checked every leg's mark through the 2026-08-14 close plus the macro tape.

MACRO: S&P 500 set a record above 7,800 midweek and closed the week -0.2% but with a third straight weekly gain. July CPI +0.1% m/m, headline 3.4%, core 2.5% — in line; PPI headline flat, core +0.2%, below expectations. The dovish repricing I bought PEG for did in fact arrive. UMich preliminary August sentiment softened, which capped Friday.

XLE SHORT — PREMISE BROKEN. Energy went from the week's worst sector to the week's best, +7.8%, now +38% YTD, on the US resuming/extending the Strait of Hormuz naval blockade. Brent rose from ~$82.15 (8/7) to close $88.52 on 8/14 (+1.7% Friday alone) after Treasury Secretary Bessent said the blockade of Iranian ports could run "indefinitely." An Iran-Oman reopening deal was reported near and then collapsed as ship attacks persisted. Hormuz traffic is still ~5% of pre-conflict levels and OPEC spare capacity is down to ~2.5M bpd. My entire stated edge was "XLE is discounting a crude price that no longer exists" — crude closed that gap by rising to XLE rather than XLE falling to crude. XLE ~$61.06 on 8/13 vs $57.50 on 8/7. The Hormuz tail I explicitly named as the reason for the tight -15% stop is now the base case, not a tail.

APP. $312.67 on 8/14, down ~9.8% from $346.80, a fresh 52-week low of $303.17 and now -58% from the $745.61 high, >50% down in 2026. Bank of China cut to Hold on 8/11. Fundamentals unchanged and still good: Q2 revenue $1.923B (-0.94% vs consensus), net income $1.27B +54.5%, adj EBITDA margin 84%, Q3 guided $2.055-2.085B = +46-48% y/y, CEO Foroughi attributing the shortfall to the next model step-up landing just after quarter end. No reversion trigger — it made new lows, it did not reclaim them.

HONA. $166.36 on 8/14 vs $168.51 on 8/7, but the 52-week range low has reset to $150.03, ~11% below Friday's close — the washout low was made and reclaimed inside my holding period. BMO cut to $209, Wells Fargo to $195, Jefferies to $175 on 8/10; all still well above spot. Cause unchanged: precision-casting shortage deferring aftermarket revenue, not demand loss.

WMT. $116.17, +3.9% on the week. Q2 confirmed for 8/20 before the open, consensus $0.73 EPS on $186.3B.

AXP $342.48, unchanged. TSLA $342.27, +0.7% Friday on a TD Cowen buy reiteration at $460; the higher-low sequence off $298.32 is intact. SNPS ~$412, flat on the week; Q3 FY26 confirmed for 8/26 after the close. PEG $76.04 — sitting on its 52-week low despite CPI/PPI both cooperating, i.e. my catalyst fired and the stock did not respond.

NEW CANDIDATE — CSCO. This is structurally the same setup as my AXP thesis — a beat-and-raise sold on a secondary line item — in a ~$440B mega cap with a dividend.
